units.translation: Who is this who goes about the house?
en thyo nihil est insoliti: mire vero cum accusativo sine praepositione construxit Aeschylus frequentandi sensu

as Homer says πολιὴν ἅλα [the gray sea] and πολιὴν θάλασσαν [the gray sea], others have said other such things, collected in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1344. Catullus used the verb incanesco at 61, 13 tortaque remigio spumis incanuit unda [and the wave, churned by the oar, grew white with foam]. Schol. exp. άφριζο-μένης τῷ ἀφρῷ τῆς κωπηλασίας [foaming with the foam of the rowing].
the sea growing gray with the raging wind
foaming with the foam of the rowing
It is said properly of people: improperly it means old.
who with gray law makes straight the fate
holding the city, protecting, patron and guardian of the city.
πολίοχος [city-holding] said for the sake of meter
Thus Porson for πολισσούχοι [city-guardians], which in some copies was ineptly changed to πολισοῦχοι [city-guardians]. The form πολισσούχος [city-guarding] will be discussed in its place.

Thus I corrected what is in M (with ἰὼ ἰὼ [io io] omitted) θεοὶ πολιάοχοι χθονός [gods who hold the city of the land], from which in the copies was made πολισούχοι [city-guardians] or πολισσούχοι [city-guardians].
O great Zeus and city-guarding divinities
io io, gods who hold the city of the land
io io) gods who hold the city of the land

with genitive πόλεως [of the city] or where the meter demands πόλεος [of the city]. πόλεως [of the city] not rarely with synizesis, as in the trimeters Sept. 2 ἐν πρύμνη πόλεως [in the stern of the city]. [273] 539 572 Ag. 1412 1586. Eum. 617 [701] 704. 868. Suppl. 248 388 619 902 and at the beginning of trimeters, where it is rather an iamb than an anapest, as Sept. 471 πόλεως ἀπείργειν [to keep from the city]. and at the end of trimeters Sept. 57 ἄνδρας ἐκκρίτους πόλεως [chosen men of the city]. Ib. 1006. [Ch. 289.] More rarely in other meters. Sept. 165 προφρόνως | ἑπτάπυλον πόλεως ἕδος ἐπιρρύου [graciously protect the seven-gated seat of the city]. Ib. 418. 761. Suppl. 902. It is said not only of the city itself, but also of the state, i.e. the community of people living in the city.
May he be named after the Cadmeans
Do not utterly destroy my city from its roots
For a city faring well honors the gods
And you, blessed queen Onca, graciously the seven-gated seat of the city
Sic correxi pro Ὄγκα προ [Onca, before] (πρὸ μ. recentiori) πόλεως | ἑπτάπυλον ἕδος ἐπυρρύου [the seven-gated seat of the city, protect].
And you are mindful of the city's rites that love sacrifice
